title: Statistical questions and variability
summary: Partners sort questions as statistical or not by predicting whether the answers would vary, revise one-answer questions into survey questions, and describe the data they would collect (6.SP.B.5).

standard.text: Recognize a statistical question as one that anticipates variability in the data related to the question and accounts for it in the answers.

discourse: Argue whether a question is statistical by predicting the range of answers it would collect and giving an example of two different answers.
Revise a one-answer question into a statistical question and justify the change by naming who would be asked and what would vary.
Describe a planned data set for a reader, naming the attribute measured, its unit and how many observations there would be (6.SP.B.5).
sentence: Question forms that change the meaning: How many pets does Ana have? (one answer) versus How many pets do students in our class have? (many answers).
Claim and reason: This question is / is not statistical because the answers would / would not vary.
Hedged predictions: The answers will probably range from ___ to ___; most students might say ___.
word: The word family vary, various, variable, variability, and the everyday opposite same.
Data (many answers; data are is formal, data is is common), survey, observation, collect, attribute.
Who-words that signal a group: students in our class, people at our school, every player on the team.

contentObjective: Students will recognize statistical questions as those that anticipate variability, revise questions to make them statistical, and describe the data they would collect (6.SP.A.1, 6.SP.B.5).
languageObjective: Students will argue whether a question is statistical using because the answers would / would not vary and hedged predictions about the range of answers.

L1-2: The answers will be the same / different.
It is / is not a statistical question. (Word bank: vary, same, different, survey, data)
L3-4: This question is / is not statistical because the answers would / would not vary.
I would ask ___, and the answers might range from ___ to ___.
To make it statistical, I changed ___ to ___.
L5-6: Although this question has a number for an answer, it is not statistical, because ___.
The revised question anticipates variability, since ___; I would expect answers such as ___ and ___.
My data set would have about ___ observations of ___, measured in ___.

facts or numbers collected to answer a question

activity.title: Statistical or Not? Question Sort
steps: Write eight questions on the board: How many days are in March? How many minutes did students in our class read last night? What time does our school day start? How many hours of sleep do students in our grade get on a school night? How many windows are in our classroom? What is each student's favorite sport? What is the capital of Maryland? How many letters are in the first names of students in our class? Partners draw two columns on paper: Statistical and Not Statistical.
Partners take turns choosing a question, predicting two possible answers aloud, and writing it in the Statistical or Not Statistical column with a because sentence.
For every Not Statistical question, partners rewrite it as a statistical question and tell who they would ask and what would vary.
Partners choose one revised question and describe the data set: attribute, unit and number of observations if they asked the whole class.
Partners solve the problems below; two pairs share a revision and the class predicts the range of answers.

problems.prompt: Statistical or not: How tall is the classroom door?
problems.answer: Not statistical; there is one correct measurement, so no variability is expected.

problems.prompt: Revise this question so it is statistical: How old is Ms. Rivera?
problems.answer: Possible answer: How old are the teachers at our school? The answers will vary from teacher to teacher.

problems.prompt: A class asked, How many minutes did you read last night? The answers were 0, 15, 20, 20, 30, 45 and 60. How many observations were collected?
For the same data, what is the difference between the greatest and least answers?

warmup: Ask two questions out loud: What day is it today? and What is your favorite fruit? Students write both answers on scrap paper and hold them up. Partners compare: which question got the same answer from everyone and which got many? Introduce the words vary and variability using the papers as evidence.
